title: The services page a logistics company actually needs
metaTitle: Logistics services page, in plain words
excerpt: List each service the way an operator would say it: the outcome, the boundary, and a quote as the next step. A grid of vague capabilities does not move freight.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp, a working setup rather than a service slogan.
caption: A dim desk with two monitors, a code editor, and a lit lamp. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should each logistics service block contain?
faqs.answer: An outcome tied to a clock or a document, a boundary that names a refusal or a limit, and a quote path that asks for the facts that mode needs. Use equipment and geography an operator already says. If you cannot write those three parts, the mode is not ready to publish.

faqs.question: How many modes should a carrier list?
faqs.answer: List the modes a desk will answer for this month, often one to five. Lead with the work you want to receive. A mode you run twice a year should not sit in an equal card beside the core lane. Add a service when the first real load runs under those rules, not when the slide exists.

faqs.question: Why are capability grids a problem on a logistics site?
faqs.answer: Equal tiles hide cutoffs, refusals, and the difference between LTL and truckload. They make a rare mode look as ready as the one you run every day. Cards can still be visual. The important service should be allowed more lines, and the words should be equipment and clocks, not "end-to-end."

markdown:
The logistics company services page should list the work in an operator's language. Each service needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step, and that step is to request a quote. A grid of vague capabilities, "warehousing, distribution, technology, consulting," does not help someone move a load.

The page is a catalog of jobs you will run this month. If a mode is a slide in a deck and not a desk that answers, it is not a block yet.

## Name the job the way a dispatcher would

Start from the sentence an operator uses on the phone. "I have six pallets that have to be in Dallas Thursday." "I need a dedicated truck every Tuesday, same receiver." "I need this machine tarped, not stacked." Those sentences are the services. The brand names you gave them internally can stay off the page.

Headings should sound like those calls. "Dock-to-dock LTL." "Dedicated dry van." "Flatbed with tarps." "Cross-dock and out the same night," if you truly turn freight the same night. "Supply chain solutions" is not a heading. It is a way to avoid choosing.

Google's people-first content guidance asks whether a page lets someone do what they came to do, and whether it shows knowledge rather than slogans. An operator came to see if you haul their freight under rules they can live with. A block that names the equipment, the cutoff, and the refusal does that. A block that promises seamless visibility does not, unless you also say what the visibility actually is: a status at pickup, at the terminal, and at delivery, for example.

Read the headings to someone who books freight and does not work for you. If they ask "but is that LTL or truckload," the heading is still yours.

## Outcome, boundary, next step

Use the same three parts on every block so the page can be scanned.

The outcome is what "done" means. Delivered to a dock on the appointment. POD returned the same day. Freight checked in and out of a cross-dock without a second handling charge. Do not promise a transit day you do not publish on the rate. If transit is a range, the outcome is the range.

The boundary is the limit. Maximum weight. The states. Freight you refuse. Whether the trailer is live-load or drop. Whether you staff the unload. A service that says "white glove" and does not say who carries the freight up a flight of stairs will be heard as the more generous version. Write the narrower truth.

The next step is request a quote, with the facts that service needs. A flatbed quote needs length and a description of securement. An LTL quote needs class or a clear description, piece count, and weight. Put those prompts in the block. A single generic "Request a quote" under every card, going to a blank form, throws away the boundary you just wrote.

Use this check before a block ships:

- The heading is a phrase an operator already says.
- The outcome names a document or a clock, not a feeling.
- The boundary names a refusal or a limit.
- The quote link says which facts that mode needs.

A block that fails a line is a capability tile. Hold it.

## How many services to publish

Four or five modes is a lot for a site that wants to be believed. If you run one mode well, publish one block and a short note on what you will not do. Adding parcel, air, ocean, and "consulting" because the navigation looked empty will attract the wrong calls and weaken the right ones.

Order the blocks by the work you want the quote desk to receive. The mode that pays the week comes first. The occasional project move comes last, with a boundary that protects the desk from treating it like a standard lane.

Split by behavior, not by department. "Technology" is not a service unless an operator can buy a specific behavior: an EDI setup, a status file, a portal login with a named owner. If the technology is how you run the dock, it belongs inside the dock's block as a sentence, not as a peer of the truck.

The other readers, a broker, a receiver, a driver applicant, do not get half the grid. Give them a labeled link. Alternating cards for shippers and recruits teaches everyone to skip.

## What a capability grid hides

Six icons in two rows look finished by Thursday. They hide the cutoff, the refusal, and the difference between modes. Equal cards say equal competence. If flatbed is a favor you do twice a month, an equal card is a false ad.

Tiles also collapse accessorials into the word "flexible." Flexible is how detention becomes a fight. The services page can point at the pricing page for the charges and still say, in the block, which extras are common for that mode. A residential LTL block that never mentions a liftgate is saving a surprise.

If the visual system wants cards, let the important mode have more lines. Sameness is not a brand rule worth keeping when it makes a dedicated fleet and a rare hotshot look identical. Design can carry hierarchy. Copy has to demand it.

Watch the template words: end-to-end, turnkey, best-in-class, partner of choice. Replace each with equipment, a region, or a clock. The sentence will sound less like a logistics site from a theme, and more like a desk.

## One block, written out

Heading: Appointment LTL, dock to dock.

Outcome: We pick up on the date you confirm, move the freight through our linehaul, and deliver on the appointment window we quote. You get a POD the day it delivers.

Boundary: Business addresses with a dock in the states we list. No households, no job sites, no hazmat. Palletized freight we can count. If the description or the weight changes, the rate changes before the truck rolls, not after, and we will tell you. We do not unload by hand.

Next step: Request a quote with origin, destination, ready date, pallet count, weight, and a description. Quotes in before 2pm on a business day get a rate the same day.

That is longer than an icon. It is also enough for a coordinator to know whether to bother. Change the nouns for reefer, flatbed, or a pool distribution run. Keep the three parts. If the desk does not yet return PODs the same day, do not write that they do. Write the true clock.

## Services to leave off until they are real

A mode you are "looking into." A control tower you cannot staff. A sustainability calculator with no method. A customer portal that is a shared inbox with a logo. These can be projects. They are not services an operator can buy.

When a service becomes real, add it in the same shape, the week the first load runs under those rules. Do not pre-announce it on the page to make the company look broader. Breadth is the claim operators punish first, because breadth without a cutoff is how freight sits.

Match the block to the pricing page in one pass. If the service promises a same-day quote, the price page's clock has to match. If the service refuses residential, the accessorial list should not imply you are eager for it. Contradictions read as a company that does not talk to itself, which is a risk when the freight is already late.

## Hold the page against the last ten quotes

Pull ten recent quotes, including two you declined. Sort them by the heading on the services page. If a quote does not fit any heading, you either need a block or you need to stop quoting that work until you can describe it. If a heading has no quote in the pile, the block is a wish. Remove it or rewrite it as a limit: "We do not quote household goods."

Read the declined quotes for the reason you said no. That reason should already be a boundary on the page. Every decline that surprised the operator is a sentence you have not published. Add the sentence. The page gets more useful as your no becomes visible.

Then ask the person who answers the phone to mark any heading they would not say out loud. Those headings go. A services page the desk is embarrassed to read will be paraphrased on every call, and the paraphrase will drift from the site within a month.

Do this on the production page, not in the doc. A heading that wrapped into a slogan in the design, or a boundary that was cut "for space," is the version the operator sees. If the three parts do not survive the layout, the layout yields. Space is not a reason to turn a refusal into a tooltip.

Who stands behind those blocks is the next page a careful operator opens. That is [how a logistics company should write an about page](/blog/how-a-logistics-company-should-write-an-about-page).
